titleEn: Book of the Dead of Ani — Spell 1, second half
work: Book of the Dead of Ani
workEn: Book of the Dead of Ani
draftNote: Draft — the hieroglyphs are read from the printed type of Budge's 1895 edition of the papyrus, and the signs and readings are still being checked; expect changes.
source: Papyrus of Ani (British Museum EA 10470), Plates V, VI. Hieroglyphs transcribed from the interlinear text of E. A. W. Budge, The Book of the Dead: The Papyrus of Ani in the British Museum (London, 1895), pp. 20–24; Budge's transliteration and word-by-word English were used to check the reading of the signs and the sense, never for wording. Only the papyrus's own text is given: the passages Budge supplies from other papyri in his appendixes and footnotes are left out. Transliteration in the Leiden convention, with the reed written i; translation made fresh from the Egyptian. Shown left to right; the papyrus is written in columns read from the top down. The line under each word ("say") is the conventional Egyptological classroom pronunciation — a neutral e between consonants; ꜣ and ꜥ as a; w as u or w; ṯ as tj; ḏ as dj; ḫ and ẖ as kh; š as sh — an artificial teaching pronunciation, since the vowels of Egyptian were never written. The grouping of signs within a word follows Budge's type, which regularises the scribe's hand.
about: The second half of Spell 1 continues the speech that opens the long run of spells on the papyrus. Having spoken in the words of Thoth, the dead man now names himself a son of Busiris and lists the rites of Osiris in which he takes part, at Busiris, Rosetau, Letopolis, Heliopolis, Memphis and Herakleopolis, as priest and beside Horus. Three addresses, partly in red, then call on the gods who usher the souls of the dead into the house of Osiris, feed them and open the roads to it, asking that Ani may go in and out freely; the spell ends with the balance cleared of any case against him. This part runs from Plate 5, line 13, to Plate 6, line 44.

sentences.n: The second half of the speech begins, still in black. ink 'I' is the pot, the basket k and the seated man, as in the first half. The name ḏdy is written twice: the ḏd-pillar doubled, two reeds y and a seated god. The pillar is the sign of Busiris, ḏdw (Djedu), and the second pillar repeats the first and is not read again. The reeds are the ending -y of a nisba, an adjective made from a noun: ḏdy 'he of Busiris' (Budge: Ṭeṭṭeṭi). sꜣ 'son' is the pintail duck with a stroke, and sꜣ ḏdy is a direct genitive. The god of Busiris is Osiris and his son is Horus: the speaker now takes the part of the son.

sentences.i: I was conceived in Busiris, I was born in Busiris.
sentences.n: The papyrus writes iw-w with a seated woman, then i-m with a seated man (Budge: āu àm-à); read iwr·i 'I was conceived', a passive sḏm·f like msy·i. The hartebeest iw (E9) with the chick w as complement and the woman as classifier is the verb iwr 'conceive' without its r; the reed i and the owl m before the man have no place in it and may be the following m written too soon. Budge's two groups are joined here as one word. The parallel msy·i m ḏdw makes the sense sure, but how the extra signs arose is not. msy·i 'I was born' is the three fox-skins ms with s as complement, two reeds for the weak ending, a woman giving birth (coded B3, approximate) and ·i: the passive sḏm·f of msi. ḏdw 'Busiris' is the doubled pillar with the hand d as complement, the chick w and the town sign. Busiris, in the Delta, was the chief city of Osiris in the north.

sentences.i: I am with the mourners and the wailing women of Osiris in the Two Banks(?) of Rekhtet(?),
sentences.n: wn·i 'I am' is the hare wn with water n and ·i: the sḏm·f of wnn 'be'; 'I was' is as possible. ḥꜣyw 'the mourners' is doubtful: a papyrus stem with drooping buds (coded M16, ḥꜣ, from its shape), the vulture ꜣ, two reeds y, a bowed man (A16, approximate), a seated man and a stroke: a plural noun from ḥꜣi 'mourn', its w not written (Budge: ḥai). iꜣkbyt 'the wailing women' is i, ꜣ, the basket k, the foot b, two reeds and t, with a lock of hair (D3, doubtful), the classifier of mourning, and a seated woman. wsir follows without n: a direct genitive. Budge leaves the next group unread ('....'); it is divided here into two words, both doubtful. The first looks like the tongue of land iḏb (N21) over a canal, written twice: iḏbwy 'the Two Banks', a dual; Budge's footnote variants differ here. The second, two knotted cords (coded V1, approximate), t and the town sign, writes no r or ḫ; a footnote variant spells r-ḫ-t-t with the same cords, so it is read rḫtt, a place not identified (Budge: Reχtet). Wailing women, above all Isis and Nephthys, mourned Osiris in the rites of his death.

sentences.n: smꜣꜥ-ḫrw 'who make true of voice' is the bolt s, the sickle mꜣ under the plinth mꜣꜥ (printed as one ligature), the oar ḫrw and the chick w; the arm ꜥ and the classifier of the first half are left out. sentences.l: commanded(?) · it · Ra · Thoth · who-makes-true-of-voice · Osiris · against · enemies-his
sentences.i: Ra commanded(?) it: it is Thoth who makes Osiris true of voice against his enemies.
sentences.n: Budge leaves the first group unread ('....'). It is a staff with a loop at its foot, the sign wḏ (coded V25, approximate), with a horned viper f joined to its top. It is read wḏ 'command' here, a sḏm·f, and the reading is doubtful: wḏ is usually completed by the cobra ḏ, and the viper may stand for it, or the group may be another word. st 'it' is the bolt s and t with plural strokes: the dependent pronoun, object of the verb. A pronoun object comes before a noun subject, so rꜥ 'Ra', the seated god with the sun on his head, follows it. ḏḥwty smꜣꜥ-ḫrw wsir then says what was commanded: a noun and a participle with no suffix, 'it is Thoth who makes Osiris true of voice' (the classical language would put in before the noun), like 'I am Thoth, who makes Osiris true of voice' in the first half. smꜣꜥ-ḫrw has the man with hand to mouth as classifier here, and wsir is written with the seat first. Ra, king of the gods, orders the trial.

sentences.n: wn·i ḥnꜥ 'I am with', as in line 15. ḥr 'Horus' is the falcon with a seated god. hrw 'on the day' (the courtyard h, the mouth r, the chick w, the sun and a stroke) stands as an adverb of time and governs the infinitive after it: 'the day of clothing'. ḥbs 'clothing' is the wick ḥ, the foot b, the bolt s and a tall fringed cloth (coded S28) as classifier. tštš is t and the pool š written twice, with the seated god: a name of Osiris (Budge: Teśteś), not explained here. sentences.n: sš 'opening' is the bolt s and the pool š, with a small cross (Z9) and the papyrus roll as classifiers: sš 'open, spread open', said of doors (Budge: 'unbolting'). rꜣ is the mouth with a stroke: 'mouth', and so 'opening, door'. n 'of'. The next word is doubtful: the bolt s, the pool š, two reeds y and t, with the roll and plural strokes (Budge: seśit). No word sšyt is known to this edition; it may stand for sštꜣ 'secret, mystery' (s with štꜣ 'hidden', the word of line 26) without its ꜣ. rꜣ-sṯꜣw 'Rosetau' is the mouth rꜣ with a stroke, the drag-rope sṯꜣ (V2), a stroke, plural strokes and the desert-hill sign (N25). Rosetau is the realm of Sokar in the cemetery of Memphis, where the body of Osiris was said to lie hidden.

sentences.i: I am with Horus, guarding that left shoulder of Osiris which is in Sekhem.
sentences.n: m with an infinitive is 'in the act of': nḏ 'protect' is the sign nḏ (coded Aa27, approximate), then the pot nw, which is not read, and the low sign U15 as classifier. qꜥḥ is the hill-slope q, the arm ꜥ, the wick ḥ, a bent arm (D41), a stroke and a small sign coded F51 (flesh); it is read 'shoulder', and both the last sign and the exact sense (shoulder or arm) are doubtful (Budge: qāḥ). pwy 'that' (p, w, two reeds) follows its noun. iꜣby 'left' is doubtful too: its first sign is printed like the ankh (S34) where the chisel ꜣb (U23) is expected; with the foot b, two strokes y and the bent arm it gives ꜣby, the nisba iꜣby 'left' without its reed (Budge: àbi). imy 'which is in' is written as in the first half. sḫm 'Sekhem', Letopolis (Budge: Seχem), is the bolt s, the placenta ḫ, the sign m (Aa15), a bar with arrow-heads coded R22 (the emblem ḫm, approximate and doubtful) repeating ḫm, a house sign and the town sign. Cities of Egypt each claimed a part of the body of Osiris, which Seth had cut up and scattered.

sentences.n: wꜥb 'wab-priest, pure one' is water pouring from a vase over a foot (D60), a word-sign, with water (N35A) and a seated man as classifiers: the ordinary priest, who had to be pure to serve. The next word is not known: the mouth r and a recumbent lion (E23, rw) over a stroke, with the seated god. Read by their values the signs give rrw, or rw 'lion' with r as complement before it; Budge reads Rere and marks it with a query. The translation leaves a gap. imy pr wsir 'who is in the house of Osiris': pr is the house sign with a stroke. sqꜣ is the bolt s, the hill-slope q (Budge's numeral 26 stands after it), the vulture ꜣ and two reeds, which are not read, with a man raising both arms (A28), the roll, the seated god and a stroke: sqꜣ 'raise up, make high', the causative of qꜣi 'be high'. tꜣ 'the earth' is the strip of land with grains (N16), a word-sign. What rite 'raising up the earth' was is not known, and whether it describes the priest or the god is not clear; the reading is doubtful.

sentences.n: The papyrus writes rdit with the plain arm ꜥ (D36); read the giving arm di (D37): rdit 'placing', the infinitive of rdi. wr 'great' and ḫrp 'director' (the sceptre S42; plural not written) begin a title. The next sign, coded U23 (Budge: āb, 'the work'), is taken here for the similar drill ḥm (U24), which with the seated man gives ḥmwt 'craftsmen' and the title wr ḫrp ḥmwt 'Greatest of the Directors of Craftsmen', borne by the high priest of Ptah at Memphis; the reading of the sign is doubtful. ḥnw is the wick ḥ, water n, the pot nw and the chick w; a hoe-like sign (U6, approximate) after the wick is not read. skr 'Sokar' is s, k and r with a boat on a sledge (coded P3, approximate) as classifier. ḥnw skr is a direct genitive, Sokar's sacred boat. mꜥḫꜣyt·f is doubtful: the owl m, the arm ꜥ, a stalk with a curled top (coded M12, ḫꜣ, approximate), ꜣ, two reeds, t and a sledge (U15) as classifier, then t, w, ·f and a seated god, which are not explained; 'its sledge' follows the classifier. At the feast of Sokar the Henu-bark was set on its sledge and drawn round the walls of Memphis.

sentences.l: may-hear-he · you · may-see-he · as · see-you · may-stand-he · as · stand-you · may-sit-he · as · sit-you
sentences.i: May he hear you(?); may he see as you see, stand as you stand, sit as you sit.
sentences.n: Four wishes in the sḏm·f, each with ·f 'he'. sḏm·f 'may he hear' is the ear sḏm (coded F21) with m as complement and the roll. After it the papyrus has only t, water n and plural strokes. As it stands this is ṯn, the dependent pronoun 'you', object of the verb: 'may he hear you'. Budge's footnote corrects the passage to sḏm·f mi sḏm·tn 'may he hear as you hear', the pattern of the three clauses that follow, which would mean the scribe left out mi sḏm. Both are possible; the translation keeps what stands and marks the doubt. mꜣꜣ·f 'may he see' (eye, sickle, two vultures; Budge's numeral 33 stands inside it), mi 'as, like' (a pot in a net, W19, with the reed), mꜣꜣ·tn 'you see'. ꜥḥꜥ 'stand' is the mast P6 with the arm ꜥ and walking legs. ḥms 'sit' is a bowl with a pointed rim, coded N41 (ḥm) as the nearest shape, with the bolt s and a squatting figure; the identification is doubtful. The dead man asks to move as freely as the gods do.

sentences.i: O you who give bread and beer to the effective bas in the house of Osiris,
sentences.n: The papyrus writes this line in red as far as pr; wsir is black. ddyw 'who give' is two giving arms (D37, each d), two reeds y, the chick w and a stroke: the plural participle of rdi, which uses the stem dd. t 'bread' is t with an oval loaf crossed by lines (coded X4) and a conical loaf in a basket (coded X8), both approximate, and plural strokes; Budge reads tau, and the loaves make the reading doubtful. ḥnqt 'beer' is the beer jug (coded W22, approximate) with plural strokes, a word-sign. Bread and beer are paired without 'and', as usual. n bꜣw mnḫw m pr wsir as in line 30, here 'in' the house. Bread and beer stand for all the food the dead need.

sentences.n: di·tn 'give' is the giving arm di with ·tn: a sḏm·f wish, 'may you give', or an imperative with ·tn added. t and ḥnqt as before. trwy 'the two seasons', morning and evening, is the plant tr (M6) with t and r before it as complements and a reed (not read) between, then the chick w and two strokes y, with two suns: the dual of tr 'time, season'. bꜣ is written here with a kneeling man (coded A2) as classifier. ḫr 'before, in the presence of' is the placenta ḫ and the mouth r. nṯrw nbw 'all the gods' is the god's flag three times and the basket nb with plural strokes. ꜣbḏw 'Abydos' (Budge: Àbṭu) is a single emblem, the fetish of the city on its pole (coded R17, approximate), with none of the signs that spell the name. sentences.i: O you who open the way and open the roads to the effective bas in the house of Osiris,
sentences.n: The papyrus writes this line in red as far as n 'of'; wsir is black. wnyw 'who open' is the hare wn, water n, two reeds y and the chick w, with the door-leaf (O31) and the low sign U15 as classifiers: a plural participle of wn 'open'. wꜣt 'the way' is the road with shrubs (N31), t and a stroke. wpyw 'who open, who part' is the horns wp (F13) with p and w as complements, two reeds y, a small cross (Z9), walking legs and a stroke: a plural participle of wpi (Budge: àpui). mṯnw 'the roads' is doubtful (Budge: mātennu): the owl m joined to an arm (coded G17 + D36, approximate), t, water n, the pot nw and the chick w, with the road sign and plural strokes; it is read as the plural of mṯn 'road', with t written for ṯ and the arm not read. Opening the ways is the office of Wepwawet, 'Opener of the Ways', whose name uses the same verb and noun as wpyw … wꜣt.

sentences.i: open, then, the roads to the ba of the Osiris, the accounting scribe of the god's offerings of all the gods, Ani, with you.
sentences.n: wp 'open' is the horns wp with p and w as complements, the small cross and the roll: the imperative of wpi. irf·tn and mṯnw as before; Budge's numeral 39 stands before the road sign. wsir is written eye first. sš ḥsb, the palette sš and the sign ḥsb (coded Aa2, approximate) with the roll, is the title 'accounting scribe'. Budge's groups neter and ḥetepu are joined here as one word, ḥtp-nṯr 'god's offerings': the flag nṯr, written first out of respect, and the offering table ḥtp. The flag stands in square brackets in Budge's hieroglyphs: it is restored where the papyrus is damaged. nṯrw nbw 'of all the gods' follows as a direct genitive, and ꜣny closes the title without mꜣꜥ-ḫrw. Ani's title says he kept the accounts of the temple offerings.

sentences.i: May he go in with […] and come out in peace from the house of Osiris.
sentences.n: ꜥq·f 'may he go in' and pr·f 'may he come out' are sḏm·f wishes with ·f. m 'with'. The next word is the hand d, water n and the hand d again with a horned bull's head (coded F1, approximate): dnd. A word dnd 'rage, wrath' may be meant, but whether it is written so cannot be checked here, and rage does not suit the wish; Budge's 'confidence' is a guess from the sense. The translation leaves a gap. m ḥtp 'in peace': ḥtp is the offering table, a word-sign, with t and p as complements and the roll. m 'from'. To go in and out of the world below at will is what the spells of going forth by day promise.

sentences.n: n 'not' is the arms of negation (D35) with water n as complement, before the passive sḏm·tw·f. ḫsf 'repel' is the spindle with the horned viper joined to it (U35), a single sign, with the low sign U15; then t and w, the tw of the passive, and ·f. šnꜥ 'turn back' is the loop šn (V7) with n, the arm ꜥ and walking legs; a recumbent lion (E23) after the arm is not read (Budge: śenār, taking it for r). n with the sḏm·f mostly denies the past ('he was not repelled'); but n is often written for nn in copies of this time, and among the wishes the future of nn fits: 'he shall not be repelled'. sentences.i: No fault of his can be found there.
sentences.n: n 'not', as before. gm·n·tw is the ibis gm (G28) with m as complement, water n of the sḏm·n·f, and t and w: the passive sḏm·n·tw·f of gmi 'find', with the noun subject after it. n with the sḏm·n·f does not, in the classical language, state a past act (that is n with the sḏm·f); it says what does not or cannot happen, as in the weighing of the heart: 'no fault of his can be found'. In copies of this time it may also stand for the past, 'has not been found'. wn·f 'his fault' is the hare wn with n and the small bird of bad things (G37), and ·f; the hare, water and bird stand in square brackets in Budge's hieroglyphs, restored where the papyrus is damaged. This wn 'fault, failing' is a different word from wn 'open'. im 'there' (reed and owl): in the hall of judgment.

sentences.l: the-balance · is-emptied · of · case-his
sentences.i: The balance is cleared of his case.
sentences.n: The papyrus writes s-s-w with the bird of bad things; read sšw, with the second s standing for š, and the reading is doubtful (Budge: sesu-θà, 'have been emptied'). iw (reed and chick) opens the statement and is not translated. mḫꜣt 'balance' is doubtful in the print too (Budge: māχat): the owl m with an arm joined to it, as in mṯnw, not read; a post with a loop on top (coded U39) where the sign ḫꜣ is expected (cf. line 29); the vulture ꜣ, t, two strokes and the balance (U38) as classifier. sšw is the causative of šwi 'be empty', 'make empty', in the stative with its third feminine ending ·ṯi (V13 ṯ and the reed), agreeing with mḫꜣt: 'is emptied'. m 'of'. sp·f 'his case, his deed' is the bolt s and the stool p as complements, the threshing floor sp (O50) and ·f; the viper is in square brackets, Budge's restoration. Nothing is left in the scale against him. The spell ends here.
